title: Being done, not doing
goal: Turn sentences into the passive in three tenses, name the doer with a or ab, and recognize deponent verbs that look passive but mean active.
bekal: tell a doer (*a fabris*) from a tool (*equis*)
not be surprised by *loquitur*, which looks passive but means "he speaks"

dialogs.title: Colloquium — Thermae novae
dialogs.intro: Beside the main road, public baths are being built. Marcus wants to know everything.

lines.speaker: Quintus:
lines.text: Thermae novae aedificantur. A civibus amantur!
lines.id: New baths are being built. The citizens love them!
lines.literal: baths-pl new-pl be-built-they. by citizen-pl-by be-loved-they!

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.id: Who are they being built by?

lines.speaker: Quintus:
lines.text: A fabris. Lapides ex montibus portantur.
lines.id: By the builders. The stones are carried from the mountains.
lines.literal: by builder-pl-by. stone-pl from mountain-pl-from be-carried-they.

lines.speaker: Iulia:
lines.id: How are they carried? By horse?

lines.speaker: Quintus:
lines.text: Equis et navibus portantur. Via Appia longa est.
lines.id: By horse and by ship. The Via Appia is long.
lines.literal: horse-pl-with and ship-pl-with be-carried-they. road Appian long-fem is-it.

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.text: Et aqua? Unde aqua in urbem ducitur?
lines.id: And the water? Where is the water brought into the city from?
lines.literal: and water? from-where water into city-obj be-led-it?

lines.speaker: Quintus:
lines.text: Per aquaeductum ducitur. Opus mirum est!
lines.id: It's brought through an aqueduct. An amazing piece of work!
lines.literal: through aqueduct-obj be-led-it. work amazing-neut is-it!

lines.speaker: Iulia:
lines.text: Ego quoque aedificare volo. Sed a matre non sinor.
lines.id: I want to build too. But Mom won't let me.
lines.literal: I too build want-I. but by mother-by not be-allowed-I.

lines.speaker: Cornelia:
lines.text: Parva es adhuc, Iulia. Sed olim docebis me!
lines.id: You're still little, Iulia. But one day you'll teach me!
lines.literal: small-fem are-you still, Iulia. but one-day teach-you-will me-obj!

lines.speaker: Marcus:
lines.id: Father, when will the baths open?

lines.speaker: Quintus:
lines.text: Post duos annos aperientur. Tum omnes lavabimur!
lines.id: In two years. Then we'll all bathe there!
lines.literal: after two-obj year-pl-obj be-opened-they-will. then all-pl be-washed-we-will!

notes: **Aedificat becomes aedificatur.** The passive ending is an *-r* added to the ordinary person ending, sometimes with a small change: *-o* → *-or*, *-t* → *-tur*, *-nt* → *-ntur*. That's why most passive forms feel one syllable heavier, and they're easy to spot from a distance.

**A fabris but equis.** If the doer is a **person**, Latin puts *a* or *ab* in front: *a fabris*, *a matre*, *a civibus*. If it's a **tool or means**, the preposition is dropped completely: *equis portantur* ("carried by horse"), *gladio vulneratur* ("wounded with a sword").

**Thermae is always plural.** Some Latin words have no singular at all: *thermae* (public baths), *castra* (camp), *litterae* in the sense of a letter, *arma* (weapons), *divitiae* (wealth). Adjectives and verbs with them must be plural too, even when one building is meant.

**Sinor — the passive "I" form ends in -or.** Iulia says *non sinor*, "I am not allowed". Note that this *-or* looks exactly like the ending of nouns such as *mercator* and *doctor*. The resemblance is a coincidence — the passive ending and the doer-noun ending come from two different sources — so don't mix them up: *mercator* is a noun, *sinor* is a verb.

blocks.text: Six passive endings are used in every group and in every tense you've learned, except the perfect. Learn the six just once.

Look at the passive infinitive. Groups I, II, and IV just swap *-re* for *-ri*: *amare* → *amari*. Group III shrinks all the way: *mittere* → *mitti*, *legere* → *legi*, *duci* from *ducere*. This form shows up in sentences like *Amari volo* — "I want to be loved".
Turning an active sentence into a passive one swaps two roles: the object becomes the subject, and the old subject moves behind *a* or *ab*.

Translation
rows: The wall is being built by the builder.
The pupils are praised by the teacher.
The baths are loved by the citizens.
The stones are carried by horse.
The city is saved by water.

blocks.text: The last two rows show the rule people forget most: horses and water aren't people, so both stand without a preposition. If you write *ab equis*, the sentence changes to "by the horses as conscious doers" — something that only makes sense in a fairy tale.

blocks.title: Why Latin so often chooses the passive
items: Because the doer is unimportant or unknown: *dicitur* — "it is said", "they say".
Because the thing itself is what matters: *thermae aedificantur* puts the focus on the building, not the builders.
Because official writing sounds that way. Roman laws, inscriptions, and announcements are almost entirely passive — much like legal English today.
*Videtur* has a special, very common meaning: not "he is seen" but "it seems". *Mihi videtur* — "it seems to me".

sections.title: The perfect passive, and deponent verbs

blocks.text: For the perfect, Latin doesn't use passive endings at all. It uses two words: an adjective form of the verb, plus *sum*. That adjective form changes its endings like *bonus*.

This adjective form — called a participle — comes from the fourth part of the dictionary form: *amo, amare, amavi, **amatum***. It's studied fully at the next level, but you already know many of them as English words: *fact* from *factum*, *dictum* from *dictum*, *data* from *datum*, *script* from *scriptum*.
Verbs that look passive but mean active

Verbs like these are called deponents — literally "having laid aside" their active form. There aren't many, but they're common, and you already know their traces: *sequitur* gives *sequence* and *consequence*, *nascitur* gives *natal* and *nation*, *patitur* gives *patient* and *passive*.
